title: Chitrakoot
hook: the exiles reach the mountain, build a hut of leaves, and meet the poet who is telling their story

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharadvaja, part two. A raft across the Yamuna, the dark banyan, and a mountain of peacocks and honey. Did you give a landmark a breath? Today they arrive, and the week closes. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

The forest is in flower. Rama walks with Sita, and for the first time since Ayodhya, he sounds almost happy. Look, he tells her, the flame-of-the-forest trees are in bloom, so red they look like they're on fire. Look at the honeycombs hanging from the branches, as big as buckets. Listen to the birds. Then the trees open up, and there it is ahead of them: a mountain with many peaks, streams running down its sides. Chitrakuta.
screen: `THE FOREST IN FLOWER.` → `TREES THAT LOOK ON FIRE.` → `THERE IT IS: CHITRAKUTA.`

segments.voice: Chitrakuta, or Chitrakoot as many people say it today, means something like the bright peak, or the many-colored peak. And it lives up to its name. Rama decides at once: we'll live here. But first, a visit. On the mountain, the text says, is the hermitage of a sage, and the three exiles go and bow to him. The sage is Valmiki. Stop and enjoy that. The poet who is telling us this whole story appears inside it, welcoming the hero he's writing about. The Ramayana does this from its first pages: Valmiki hears Rama's story from Narada, and later in the epic, Sita's sons will grow up in his hermitage. Here, he simply greets them, and they sit with him for a while. Then the work. Lakshmana goes into the forest and gathers wood and leaves, and builds a hut, a parnashala, a house of leaves, strong enough against wind and rain, with a door and a thatched roof. Before they move in, Rama performs a rite to bless the house, as a family would for a new home, offering to the gods of the dwelling. Then Rama, Sita and Lakshmana step inside. And this closes a week that carried them all the way here. A chariot leaving a weeping city. A night by the Tamasa. A friend on the Ganga, a night watch, a crossing with a prayer in midstream. A sage at the meeting of the rivers. A raft, a dark banyan, and now a home made of leaves, on a bright mountain, with a poet next door.
screen: `CHITRAKUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.` · `VALMIKI, INSIDE HIS OWN STORY.` · `A PARNASHALA, A HOUSE OF LEAVES.` · `A BLESSING FOR THE NEW HOME.` · then, large: `A WEEK FROM A CITY TO A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think about the place you live. Not the whole building, just one corner of it: a chair, a window, a doorway. Picture it the way Rama and Sita saw their hut the first night, small and new and theirs. Breathe in, and feel gratitude for having a roof. Breathe out, and wish the same for someone who doesn't. If you pray, you can bless your home in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Chitrakoot. The bright mountain where the exiles meet Valmiki, and Lakshmana builds a house of leaves that becomes their first home in the forest.
Your line: Chitrakoot. Today, when you walk through your own front door, pause and notice that it's home. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Hindu families hold a griha pravesha, a house-entering ceremony, before moving into a new home; in the text, Rama blesses the leaf hut at Chitrakuta before the three exiles enter it.

fork.setup: you're Rama. you've reached a beautiful mountain, there's a sage's hermitage nearby, and you need a home for the years ahead. what do you do first?
options: go and bow to the sage who lives there.
keep walking deeper into the forest.
fork.reveal: they first pay respects at Valmiki's hermitage, then Lakshmana builds the leaf hut, and Rama blesses it.

original.note: Sanskrit parṇaśālā: a hut of leaves, parṇa (leaf) plus śālā (hall, house); the exiles' home on Chitrakuta.

trapdoor: what you thought: Valmiki only narrates the Ramayana from outside.
what it means: he appears in it, greeting Rama at Chitrakuta.
what a scholar hears: the poet appears in his own work at several points, hearing the story from Narada, meeting Rama here, and sheltering Sita later, a frame that later retellers kept.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 56 (the walk to Chitrakuta; meeting Valmiki; the leaf hut and its blessing)

notes: Sarga number follows the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
The house-blessing rite in the text (vastu offering) includes an animal offering in some versions; the script describes it only as a blessing rite. A Keeper should confirm this framing.
The flame-of-the-forest (kimshuka/palasha) and the honeycombs 'as big as buckets' (drona-sized): confirm.
Meaning of citrakūṭa (bright or many-colored peak): standard compound sense; confirm.
